q: A decision tree algorithm evaluates candidate splits at each node and picks the one that produces child nodes with the least mixed class labels. What general property is being maximized at each split?
options: Impurity reduction
Variance of the target
Total leaf count
Depth of the tree
explanation: Splitting rules such as Gini impurity and entropy/information gain both choose the split that most reduces impurity in the resulting child nodes.

q: In a churn-prediction tree, a node currently contains a 50/50 mix of churned and retained customers. After splitting on 'contract type', one child is 90% retained and the other is 85% churned. Why would a tree-building algorithm favor this split over one that leaves both children close to 50/50?
options: It produces a larger reduction in impurity across the children
It evaluates fewer candidate features, which only saves computation and does not affect purity
It produces a shallower tree structure regardless of how mixed the resulting labels are
It guarantees the identical split will be chosen again at every node beneath it
explanation: Splits that separate classes more cleanly reduce impurity more, which is exactly what criteria like Gini and entropy are designed to reward.

q: A fraud-detection tree is being built, and two criteria, Gini impurity and entropy-based information gain, are both available for choosing splits. In practice, how do the trees they produce typically compare?
options: They usually select very similar splits and produce similar-looking trees, differing mainly in computation speed
Entropy consistently yields a shallower tree than Gini because it penalizes impurity more aggressively
Gini impurity can only be applied to regression trees, since it cannot handle discrete class labels
Information gain disregards the class distribution of the child nodes and looks only at sample counts
explanation: Gini and entropy are both impurity measures that behave similarly in practice; they occasionally disagree on the single best split but generally lead to comparable trees, with Gini being cheaper to compute since it avoids logarithms.

q: Which quantity does information gain directly measure when choosing a split in a decision tree?
options: The reduction in entropy achieved by splitting on a given feature
The absolute difference in sample counts between child nodes
The correlation between two candidate features being considered for the same split
The number of distinct unique values that a given feature can possibly take
explanation: Information gain is defined as the entropy of the parent node minus the weighted entropy of the child nodes after the split.

q: In a loan-approval tree, a node is perfectly pure (all applicants are in the 'approved' class). What is the impurity of this node under either Gini or entropy, and what does that imply for further splitting?
options: Impurity is zero, so no further split can improve the node and it becomes a leaf
Impurity is at its theoretical maximum, so the algorithm is forced to search for another split
Impurity cannot be computed once a node contains only a single class label present
Impurity equals the total number of training samples routed to that particular node
explanation: A node containing only one class has zero impurity by definition, so there is nothing left to gain by splitting it further and it is turned into a leaf.

q: Which of the following best describes what entropy measures at a node in a classification tree?
options: The amount of disorder or uncertainty in the class labels present at that node
The average numeric value of the input features for samples reaching that node
The total count of training samples that happen to reach that particular node
The depth of that node measured along the path down from the root of the tree
explanation: Entropy quantifies how mixed the class labels are; it is 0 for a pure node and maximal when classes are evenly mixed.

q: A manufacturing QC tree splits on 'temperature at production' first, then on 'humidity'. If the algorithm instead evaluated 'humidity' before 'temperature' at the root and found a higher information gain there, what would happen?
options: The tree would split on 'humidity' at the root instead, since it produces the larger impurity reduction
The tree would still split on 'temperature' first because features are evaluated in input order
Both features would be combined and used simultaneously within a single multi-way split
The algorithm would ignore both candidates and instead split on a randomly chosen third feature
explanation: Greedy tree induction always picks the feature and threshold that yields the highest impurity reduction (information gain) at each node, regardless of input ordering.

q: Gini impurity for a node is lowest when ______.
options: all samples at the node belong to a single class
the node contains an equal mix of all classes
the node has the maximum possible number of samples
the feature used to reach the node is continuous rather than categorical
explanation: Gini impurity is zero for a pure node (single class) and is highest when classes are evenly mixed, so a single-class node has the lowest possible Gini.

q: A credit-scoring tree splits on 'annual income' using a threshold, while a competing split on 'number of credit lines' is rejected. What does this rejection imply about the information-gain comparison between the two candidate splits?
options: The income split produced a larger reduction in node impurity than the credit-lines split
The credit-lines feature was entirely missing from the dataset used to train this tree
The income split happened to use a smaller number of training samples at that node
The algorithm always prefers numeric features over categorical ones regardless of gain
explanation: A greedy tree-growing algorithm keeps the split with the highest information gain (or Gini reduction) among all candidates considered at that node; being rejected means it scored lower.

q: Why do many implementations default to Gini impurity rather than entropy for choosing splits in classification trees?
options: Gini avoids logarithm computations and is faster to evaluate while giving similar results
Gini is claimed to be the only impurity criterion that supports multi-class classification problems
Entropy cannot be computed at all when the splitting feature is continuous rather than categorical
Gini is claimed to guarantee a globally optimal tree, a property entropy supposedly lacks
explanation: Gini impurity uses only sums of squared proportions (no logarithms), making it computationally cheaper than entropy while typically producing comparable splits.

q: A retail tree predicting 'will purchase' considers splitting on 'store visits per month'. One threshold yields children with class proportions (80% yes, 20% no) and (30% yes, 70% no); another threshold yields (55% yes, 45% no) and (52% yes, 48% no). Which threshold would a greedy tree-building algorithm choose, and why?
options: The first threshold, because it produces a larger reduction in impurity by separating the classes more clearly
The second threshold, because it keeps a more even number of samples in each resulting child node
Both thresholds are equally good since they are candidate splits on the same underlying feature
Neither threshold is valid, because every split must always produce exactly 50/50 children
explanation: The first split creates much purer children than the second, so it yields a larger impurity reduction and would be preferred by the greedy splitting rule.

q: A decision tree for regression (predicting house prices) cannot use Gini impurity or entropy to choose splits. What does it typically minimize instead?
options: Within-node variance (or mean squared error) of the target variable
Classification accuracy computed at each resulting leaf node of the tree
The number of distinct categorical levels present in a candidate feature
The depth of the resulting subtree below the chosen split point
explanation: Regression trees choose splits that minimize the variance (or MSE) of the target values within each resulting child node, since there is no discrete class label to measure impurity over.

q: Two candidate splits in a medical-diagnosis tree achieve identical information gain but one splits on 'patient age' and the other on 'resting heart rate'. Does information gain alone determine which split a standard greedy algorithm selects in this tie?
options: No extra preference is defined by information gain itself; implementations break ties by a fixed rule such as feature order
Information gain is defined to always favor numeric features over categorical ones whenever a tie occurs, regardless of impurity
Information gain becomes mathematically undefined whenever two candidate splits tie exactly
The split on whichever feature has more missing values is always automatically preferred in a tie
explanation: Information gain only ranks splits by impurity reduction; when two candidates tie exactly, the specific tie-breaking behavior is an implementation detail, not something information gain itself specifies.

q: Which statement correctly contrasts Gini impurity and information gain (entropy-based)?
options: Both measure node impurity and tend to agree on the best split most of the time, differing in how heavily they penalize mixed classes
Gini impurity is restricted to use in regression trees only, while entropy applies only to classification trees
Information gain is computed while completely ignoring the class proportions, whereas Gini relies on them directly at every split in practice
Gini impurity can take on negative values in some cases, whereas entropy mathematically never can
explanation: Both are impurity-based criteria computed from class proportions; they usually select similar splits, though entropy penalizes highly mixed nodes slightly more steeply than Gini.

q: A decision tree trained on hospital readmission records reaches 100% training accuracy but only 65% test accuracy. What most likely explains this gap?
options: The tree was grown deep enough to memorize noise and individual training cases rather than general patterns
The tree used far too few input features to ever find any real underlying pattern
The training set contained too few rows for the algorithm to compute any valid splits
The test set apparently used a different, incompatible set of class labels than the ones used during training
explanation: A tree allowed to grow until every leaf is pure will fit noise and idiosyncrasies of the training data, memorizing it rather than generalizing, which shows up as a large train-test accuracy gap.

q: Which of the following is a direct symptom of an overfit decision tree?
options: Very high training accuracy paired with noticeably lower test accuracy
Roughly similar accuracy measured on both the training and the test sets
Low training accuracy despite having a very large labeled dataset available
A tree consisting of only a single internal node and two leaves
explanation: Overfitting is characterized by the model fitting training data (including its noise) almost perfectly while failing to generalize to unseen data.

q: A single decision tree for predicting customer churn is allowed to grow without any depth limit. What is the most likely consequence?
options: The tree keeps splitting until leaves are pure or tiny, memorizing training examples and overfitting
The tree will automatically halt itself at whatever depth best generalizes to new data
The tree becomes severely under-fit since unlimited depth reduces its effective parameters
The tree's eventual predictions become statistically independent of the training data used
explanation: Without a stopping rule, greedy tree growth continues splitting until nodes are pure or contain very few samples, which captures noise in the training set and hurts generalization.

q: Which hyperparameter, if left unconstrained, most directly allows a decision tree to overfit?
options: Maximum tree depth
The impurity criterion used (Gini vs. entropy)
The random seed used for data shuffling
The order in which features appear in the dataset
explanation: An unconstrained (unlimited) maximum depth lets the tree keep splitting until it perfectly fits the training data, which is the classic cause of overfitting in a single tree.

q: A credit-risk tree has a leaf containing exactly one training applicant who defaulted, and that leaf predicts 'default' with 100% confidence for any new applicant routed there. What practice would most directly reduce this kind of overfitting?
options: Setting a minimum number of samples required per leaf before allowing a split
Increasing the number of candidate features considered at every split decision
Switching the node impurity criterion from Gini to entropy-based information gain
Training repeatedly on many identical duplicate copies of that same applicant's record
explanation: Requiring a minimum sample count per leaf prevents the tree from creating ultra-specific leaves based on a single (possibly noisy) training example.

q: A decision tree gives 100% training accuracy but 65% test accuracy, while a random forest trained on the same data gives 82% test accuracy using the same type of base learner. Why is the forest more stable despite using identical base learners?
options: Averaging predictions across many trees, each trained on different bootstrapped data, cancels out individual overfitting
The forest trains each tree on the full dataset with no randomness, which inherently prevents overfitting
Random forests use a fundamentally different, overfitting-proof splitting criterion at every single node
The forest's individual trees are all pruned down to zero depth, which eliminates variance by construction
explanation: Each individual tree in a forest can still overfit its own bootstrap sample, but because the trees overfit to different noise, averaging their predictions cancels much of that variance, improving generalization.

q: Pruning a decision tree after it has been fully grown is primarily intended to ______.
options: remove branches that fit noise, improving generalization at the cost of some training accuracy
increase the maximum depth the tree is still allowed to grow to
guarantee that the tree still achieves exactly 100% training accuracy afterward, no matter what
convert the entire classification tree into a regression-style tree
explanation: Pruning removes branches that contribute little predictive value and mainly capture training-set noise, trading a bit of training accuracy for better generalization.

q: A single, deep decision tree used for manufacturing defect detection performs very differently depending on which random subset of the training data it is trained on. What property of decision trees does this illustrate?
options: High variance: small changes in training data can produce very different tree structures
High bias: the single tree model is far too simple to capture the real pattern
Perfect generalization, since decision trees behave deterministically given enough data
Immunity to overfitting, which is guaranteed by the tree's feature importance ranking
explanation: Unpruned decision trees are notoriously high-variance models; because splits are chosen greedily, a small change in the training sample can cascade into a very different tree.

q: Which of the following is NOT a common way to reduce overfitting in a single decision tree?
options: Increasing maximum depth without bound
Limiting the maximum depth of the tree
Requiring a minimum number of samples per leaf
Pruning branches after the tree is fully grown
explanation: Increasing maximum depth without bound does the opposite of controlling overfitting; it lets the tree keep splitting until it memorizes the training data.

q: In a churn-prediction task, a shallow decision tree (max depth 3) underperforms on both training and test accuracy, while a very deep tree (unlimited depth) gets near-perfect training accuracy but much worse test accuracy. What does this pattern describe?
options: The classic bias-variance tradeoff: the shallow tree underfits while the deep tree overfits
Both the shallow and the deep tree are overfitting the data to an equal degree
The shallow tree is overfitting while the deep tree is actually underfitting the signal
Neither tree's performance is affected by its maximum depth setting at all
explanation: A shallow tree is too simple to capture the signal (high bias, underfitting), while an unconstrained tree fits training noise too closely (high variance, overfitting) - exactly the bias-variance tradeoff.

q: Why are individual, unpruned decision trees commonly described as 'high variance, low bias' models?
options: They can fit training data very closely (low bias), but their structure shifts a lot across samples (high variance)
They systematically underfit essentially all datasets, regardless of how deep they are grown
They maintain a fixed, unchanging tree structure no matter what training data they are given
They are fundamentally incapable of representing any non-linear decision boundary in the data, regardless of depth
explanation: Deep trees can approximate complex functions and fit training data almost exactly, giving low bias, but small perturbations to the training set lead to very different trees, giving high variance.

q: A single decision tree used to flag fraudulent transactions achieves excellent accuracy on historical data but repeatedly misses new fraud patterns once deployed. Which ensemble strategy most directly targets the variance problem causing this?
options: Bagging, since it averages many trees trained on different bootstrapped samples to reduce variance
Increasing the tree's maximum depth further to fit the historical data even more closely
Removing all remaining regularization constraints from that single decision tree entirely
Switching that single tree's impurity criterion from Gini over to entropy-based information gain
explanation: Bagging directly targets high-variance base learners like unpruned trees by training many of them on different bootstrap samples and averaging, which smooths out the overfitting of any single tree.

q: A fully grown decision tree with one leaf per unique training sample is an extreme example of ______.
options: overfitting
underfitting
regularization
bootstrap aggregation
explanation: A tree with a leaf for every training example has perfectly memorized the training set, the defining extreme case of overfitting.

q: In bagging (bootstrap aggregating), each base model is trained on ______.
options: a bootstrapped sample drawn with replacement from the original training set
the exact same full original training set, left completely unchanged each time
a randomly chosen subset of features only, while every row is kept intact
only the specific samples that earlier base models happened to misclassify
explanation: Bagging draws bootstrap samples (random samples with replacement, same size as the original set) to train each base learner independently.

q: Bagging primarily reduces ______ in a model's predictions.
options: variance
bias
both bias and variance equally
irreducible error
explanation: Averaging predictions from many models trained on different bootstrap samples smooths out fluctuations from any single model, directly reducing variance, while bias stays roughly the same as a single base learner's bias.

q: A dataset has 400 samples. Using bagging with bootstrap sampling, on average how many samples will NOT appear in any given bootstrap sample used to train one tree?
explanation: As sample size grows, the probability a given sample is never drawn in n draws with replacement converges to (1 - 1/n)^n ~ 1/e ~ 0.368, so about 37% of samples are left out of any one bootstrap sample.

q: What is the term for the roughly 37% of training samples excluded from a given bootstrap sample in bagging?
options: Out-of-bag samples
Held-out validation samples
Bootstrap residuals
Orphan samples
explanation: Samples not selected into a particular bootstrap draw are called out-of-bag (OOB) samples for that base learner, and they can be used to evaluate that learner without a separate validation set.

q: A retail company bags 100 decision trees to predict whether a customer will return an item. Each tree is trained on an independent bootstrap sample of the same size as the original dataset. Why does this scheme reduce variance compared to a single tree trained on the full dataset?
options: Each tree overfits differently to the noise in its bootstrap sample, and averaging predictions cancels much of that noise
Each tree sees entirely disjoint, non-overlapping training rows, so there is no shared data between any of them
Bootstrap sampling statistically removes noise from the underlying dataset before any training ever begins
Each tree is restricted to using only a small handful of features, which by itself eliminates variance
explanation: Because each tree is trained on a different resampled version of the data, their individual errors tend to be somewhat independent; averaging many such predictions reduces the overall variance of the ensemble.

q: How are final predictions typically combined across the individual models trained in a bagging ensemble for a classification task?
options: Majority voting across the base learners' predicted classes
Taking only the first-trained base learner's prediction as the final answer
Multiplying all base learners' predicted probabilities together
Always using the base learner with the smallest training error
explanation: In classification, bagging typically aggregates base-learner predictions by majority vote; for regression, predictions are averaged instead.

q: A medical imaging team bags several models to predict whether a scan shows a tumor. Why might bagging be a good fit if the base learner (a deep, unpruned decision tree) is known to be high-variance?
options: Bagging is specifically effective at reducing the variance of high-variance, low-bias base learners through averaging
Bagging works best with already low-variance, high-bias models since it cannot help reduce variance at all in practice
Bagging completely eliminates the need for any validation of the resulting final ensemble model
Bagging automatically converts any classification base learner into a continuous regression model
explanation: Bagging is most beneficial when the base learner has high variance (like a deep, unpruned tree), since averaging many such models directly attacks the variance component of error.

q: Which statement about the base learners used in classic bagging is correct?
options: Base learners are trained independently of one another and can, in principle, be trained in parallel
Base learners must be trained sequentially, each correcting the previous one's errors
Base learners must each be trained on a disjoint, completely non-overlapping subset of rows
Base learners in classic bagging are required to always be simple linear regression models
explanation: Unlike boosting, bagging trains all base learners independently on their own bootstrap samples, so training can be fully parallelized.

q: A data scientist bags 50 identical linear regression models, each trained on a different bootstrap sample of a dataset with a strongly non-linear relationship between features and target. Why does bagging provide little benefit here?
options: Linear regression has low variance but high bias on non-linear data, and bagging mainly reduces variance, not bias
Linear regression models cannot be meaningfully bootstrapped or resampled at all for this purpose
Bagging is claimed to only work with classification models, never with regression tasks like this
Bootstrap sampling somehow removes the underlying non-linearity from the data before training starts
explanation: Bagging is most useful for high-variance base learners; a linear model underfitting a non-linear relationship suffers mainly from bias, which averaging many similar biased models does not fix.

q: In bagging, what happens to the size of each bootstrap sample relative to the original training set?
options: Each bootstrap sample is the same size as the original training set, drawn with replacement
Each bootstrap sample contains exactly half of the rows in the original training set
Each bootstrap sample is drawn to be strictly larger in size than the original dataset
Each bootstrap sample is restricted to containing only unique, non-repeated rows
explanation: A standard bootstrap sample is drawn with replacement to the same size as the original dataset, which means some original rows appear multiple times and others are left out.

q: Why can out-of-bag (OOB) samples serve as a built-in validation mechanism in a bagging ensemble, without setting aside a separate validation set?
options: Each base learner can be evaluated on the samples it never saw in training (its OOB samples), giving an unbiased estimate
OOB samples are actually treated as a separate dataset that only gets collected once training has fully completed, independent of the original data
OOB samples are simply defined as the samples associated with the highest feature importance scores
OOB evaluation actually requires completely re-training every single base learner from scratch again
explanation: Because roughly 37% of samples are excluded from each bootstrap draw, those out-of-bag samples act as a natural holdout for that specific tree, allowing OOB error estimation without a dedicated validation split.

q: A team bags 200 decision trees on a dataset of 1,000 rows. If they increase the number of trees from 200 to 2,000 while keeping bootstrap sample size fixed, what is the most likely effect on the ensemble's variance and training time?
options: Variance continues to decrease (with diminishing returns) while training time increases roughly proportionally
Variance increases substantially, since adding far more trees inevitably causes significantly more overfitting to occur
Training time stays roughly constant no matter how many additional trees are added
Variance drops all the way to exactly zero once more than 1,000 trees are used
explanation: Adding more independently trained trees to a bagged ensemble generally keeps reducing variance with diminishing returns, at the cost of roughly proportional increases in training and prediction time.

q: Bagging is best described as a technique that builds an ensemble by ______.
options: training multiple base learners in parallel on bootstrapped samples and aggregating their outputs
training a single strong learner on the entire dataset with very heavy regularization applied
training base learners sequentially, each one focusing on the previous model's errors
selecting the single best-performing model out of several candidates and discarding the rest
explanation: Bagging stands for bootstrap aggregating: training several base learners in parallel on bootstrap-resampled data, then combining (aggregating) their predictions.

q: What does the out-of-bag (OOB) error of a random forest estimate?
options: Generalization error, estimated using each tree's predictions only on samples it did not see during training
Training error, computed using only the samples that each individual tree directly saw during its own training
The error of just one single, fully pruned decision tree chosen at random
The error rate attributable only to the feature-selection step of the pipeline
explanation: OOB error aggregates, for each training sample, the predictions of only the trees that did not include that sample in their bootstrap draw, giving an estimate of generalization performance.

q: A bank builds a random forest for credit default prediction and reports an OOB error alongside a separate test-set error. Why do these two numbers often turn out to be close to one another?
options: Both estimate the same thing, generalization error, just computed on different held-out portions of the data
OOB error is always computed on the training set, so it is expected to be identical to training error
The test set and the OOB samples are mathematically required to always contain exactly the same rows
OOB error is said to only apply to regression tasks, which would make this comparison meaningless
explanation: Because OOB predictions are made only on samples each tree never saw, OOB error behaves like a built-in cross-validation estimate of generalization error, which is why it tends to track a genuine held-out test error.

q: A team wants to tune the number of trees in a random forest without setting aside an explicit validation set, since their labeled data is scarce. What built-in mechanism lets them estimate generalization performance anyway?
options: Out-of-bag error, computed from the predictions each tree makes only on the samples excluded from its own bootstrap sample
Manually running k-fold cross-validation on the entire training set again after training has already fully finished anyway
Simply using the raw training accuracy directly as a proxy for genuine test accuracy
Randomly discarding half of the trained trees and then testing only on the other half
explanation: OOB error gives a free, built-in estimate of how well the forest generalizes, since every sample has some trees that never saw it during training, removing the need for a separate validation split.

q: Approximately what fraction of the training data is available, on average, as out-of-bag samples for any single tree in a large bagging ensemble?
options: About 37%
About 63%
About 10%
About 90%
explanation: Each bootstrap sample includes about 63% of unique rows on average, leaving roughly 37% of rows out-of-bag for that tree.

q: A random forest with only 5 trees reports an OOB error, but the estimate is noticeably unstable (it changes a lot if the forest is retrained with a different random seed). Why is this expected with so few trees?
options: With few trees, each sample has very few out-of-bag trees voting on it, so its OOB prediction rests on a small, noisy subset
OOB error is mathematically undefined unless the forest contains at least 100 individual trees total
Having very few trees in the forest always produces an OOB error of exactly zero
OOB error is claimed to only work for classification problems and never for regression, explaining the observed instability here
explanation: OOB error for each sample is computed only from trees that excluded it from training; with few total trees, that subset is small, making the resulting OOB estimate noisier and more seed-dependent.

q: Why is OOB error sometimes preferred over a separate train/test split when working with a bagging-based ensemble?
options: It reuses all available data for both training and generalization estimation, without sacrificing a validation split
It is claimed to always be more accurate than any genuine, properly held-out, truly independent test-set estimate available
It completely removes the need to ever evaluate the model again after deployment
It only works correctly when the dataset contains fewer than 100 total rows
explanation: OOB error lets every row contribute to training some trees and validating others simultaneously, effectively giving a validation estimate 'for free' without holding out additional data.

q: Beyond bootstrapped row sampling like plain bagging, what additional source of randomness does a random forest introduce at each split?
options: Only a random subset of features is considered as candidates for each split
Every feature is always considered, but thresholds are chosen at random
Rows are duplicated exactly once per tree, with sampling done without replacement
The impurity criterion is randomly swapped between Gini and entropy at each node
explanation: Random forests add feature subsampling on top of bootstrap row sampling: at each split, only a random subset of the available features is considered, which decorrelates the trees.

q: A dataset has one feature, 'previous default history', that is extremely predictive of loan default, far more than any other feature. If a random forest considered all features at every split (like plain bagging with trees), what problem would likely arise?
options: Nearly every tree would split on that same dominant feature early, making the trees highly correlated and cutting the benefit of averaging
The trees would end up completely uncorrelated no matter how dominant that one feature is
The dominant feature would automatically be detected and removed from the dataset entirely
Training would fail outright, since the algorithm assumes a single feature can never be reused more than once across different trees in the forest
explanation: If every tree can always choose the single most predictive feature, most trees end up structurally similar near the root, so their errors become correlated and averaging reduces variance much less.

q: In random forest terminology, what does the parameter commonly called 'm' (or 'max_features') control?
options: The number of features randomly considered as split candidates at each node
The maximum depth that each individual tree in the forest is allowed to reach
The total number of individual decision trees included in the forest
The minimum number of samples required before a node can form a leaf
explanation: 'm' (max_features) sets how many features are randomly sampled as candidates at each split, controlling the degree of extra randomness and decorrelation introduced in a random forest.

q: A dataset has 100 features. Setting the random forest's feature-subsampling parameter m very close to 100 (i.e., almost all features considered at every split) will tend to ______.
options: make the individual trees more similar to each other, reducing the variance-reduction benefit of the forest
make the individual trees maximally diverse from one another at every split point
guarantee strictly lower training accuracy than any single standalone decision tree
force every tree in the forest to use a completely disjoint, non-overlapping feature set each and every time
explanation: As m approaches the total number of features, each tree's splits become closer to what a single, deterministic greedy tree would choose, making trees more correlated and reducing the benefit of averaging.

q: Setting m (features considered per split) very small, such as m=1 out of 50 features, in a random forest will most likely ______.
options: increase diversity between trees but may raise the bias of each tree if useful features are often excluded
always improve overall model accuracy no matter what the underlying dataset happens to look like
force every single tree in the forest to end up structurally identical to all the others
completely eliminate the need for any bootstrap row sampling in the forest whatsoever
explanation: A very small m forces more random, less-informed splits in each individual tree (raising each tree's bias), though it also maximizes decorrelation between trees; the right m balances these two effects.

q: Why does a random forest generally perform better than a single decision tree on the same data?
options: It reduces variance by averaging predictions across many decorrelated trees
It reduces bias instead, by growing a single, much deeper decision tree
It deliberately increases the variance of the ensemble's predictions on purpose
It requires collecting a smaller number of input features overall
explanation: Random forests combine bootstrap sampling and feature subsampling to grow many decorrelated trees, and averaging their predictions reduces variance substantially compared to any single tree.

q: A dataset has two features that are nearly identical copies of each other (e.g., 'annual income in USD' and 'annual income in local currency'). Why does random forest's feature subsampling help the forest handle this redundancy better than a single tree would?
options: Different trees get a chance to split on each duplicate separately instead of always relying on one, spreading their combined importance
Feature subsampling automatically detects both duplicate columns and reliably removes one of them before training even begins in practice
Redundant, duplicated features are always assigned exactly zero importance in a random forest
A single decision tree simply cannot be trained at all whenever duplicate features exist
explanation: Because each split only considers a random subset of features, some trees are forced to split on one of the redundant features instead of always defaulting to the same one, which also means their importance gets shared more realistically across both.

q: What best describes the relationship between individual trees in a well-tuned random forest?
options: They are decorrelated from one another due to row and feature randomness, even though each is trained on the same underlying dataset
They are deliberately forced to be fully identical to one another every time, purely to guarantee exact and perfect reproducibility
They are trained one after another in sequence, each correcting the previous tree's errors
They are made to share the exact same bootstrap sample and identical feature subset
explanation: The combination of bootstrap row sampling and per-split feature subsampling is specifically designed to decorrelate trees, which is what makes averaging their predictions effective at reducing variance.

q: A common default recommendation is to set m (max_features) to roughly the square root of the total number of features for classification tasks. Why would using a much larger m than this default tend to erode one of random forest's main benefits?
options: It lets most trees pick the same strongest features at the top, making them more correlated and weakening the variance benefit
It makes each tree fully deterministic and identical, so there would be no added benefit from bootstrap sampling in this scenario
It reduces the total number of training samples made available to each individual tree
It forces every single tree in the forest to be grown to an identical depth
explanation: A large m lets every tree consider nearly all features at every split, so trees tend to converge on similar strong splits, increasing correlation between trees and weakening the variance reduction that feature subsampling is meant to provide.

q: Which two sources of randomness, taken together, define how a random forest differs from simple bagging of decision trees?
options: Bootstrapped rows for each tree plus a random subset of features considered at each split
Random feature subsets for each tree plus a fixed set of rows shared across all trees
A fixed subset of rows plus a fixed subset of features, both chosen once for the whole forest
Randomly shuffled class labels combined with ordinary bootstrapped row sampling
explanation: Random forest extends plain bagging (bootstrapped rows) by also randomly restricting the candidate features considered at each split, which further decorrelates the trees.

q: A random forest trained on tabular manufacturing sensor data performs noticeably better than bagged decision trees (bootstrap rows only, all features considered at each split) trained on the same data. What is the most likely explanation?
options: The added feature subsampling decorrelates the trees further than row bootstrapping alone, giving a larger variance reduction when averaged
Random forests are claimed to always use a completely different, overfitting-proof splitting criterion than bagged trees ever use at all
Bagged trees supposedly cannot be evaluated using cross-validation, unlike random forests can
Random forests are said to not use any bootstrap sampling at all, unlike bagged trees do
explanation: The key structural difference between a random forest and plain bagging of trees is the extra random feature subsampling at each split, which reduces inter-tree correlation and typically yields a larger variance-reduction benefit.

q: For a regression random forest, how are the individual trees' predictions typically combined into a final prediction?
options: By averaging the numeric predictions from all trees
By majority vote among the trees' predicted classes
By taking only the prediction of the tree with lowest training error
By summing all trees' predictions without normalization
explanation: Regression random forests average the continuous outputs of individual trees, analogous to how classification forests use majority voting over predicted classes.

q: In a random forest, how is a feature's importance typically estimated?
options: By aggregating how much that feature reduces impurity across all the splits where it is used, across all trees
By counting how many times the feature's name appears in the dataset's column header
By measuring how strongly the feature's raw values happen to correlate with the dataset's original row index order
By checking whether the feature was the first column in the original CSV file
explanation: Feature importance in tree ensembles is usually computed from the total impurity reduction a feature contributes across all splits where it is used, averaged over all trees in the forest.

q: A churn-prediction model's feature-importance chart shows 'customer ID' as by far the most important feature, dwarfing every genuine behavioral feature. What does this most likely indicate?
options: Possible data leakage, since an identifier should have no real predictive relationship with churn
A perfectly healthy model that appears to be generalizing well to unseen, brand-new customers
That customer ID should deliberately be given even more weight in future model versions
That the underlying dataset simply contains far too few rows to train any reliable model on
explanation: An identifier dominating feature importance is a classic red flag for data leakage (e.g., IDs correlated with the target through some artifact of how the data was collected or joined) rather than a genuine causal signal.

q: A feature-importance chart for a loan-default model shows five features with roughly similar, moderate importance values and none above 25%. What does this pattern most likely suggest?
options: A reasonably healthy model where the prediction is driven by a balanced combination of signals rather than one dominant shortcut
The model has essentially and completely failed to learn anything useful at all from the training data it was given during training
Clear evidence of data leakage occurring through one specific, dominant feature
The model must actually be a single decision tree rather than a full ensemble
explanation: Balanced importance spread across several plausible features suggests the model is combining multiple genuine signals rather than relying on one dominant (and potentially leaky or spurious) feature.

q: Why can feature importance scores from a random forest be useful during exploratory data analysis, beyond just improving predictions?
options: They help identify which variables most strongly drive the outcome, supporting feature selection and domain insight
They guarantee a causal relationship between the top feature and the target
They entirely and completely replace the need for any domain knowledge whatsoever about the dataset being modeled here
They are only usable after the model has already been deployed to production
explanation: Feature importance gives a ranked view of which inputs the model relies on most, which is useful for feature selection, sanity-checking the model, and generating hypotheses, though it reflects association captured by the model rather than proven causation.

q: A manufacturing QC team trains a random forest to predict defective units and finds that 'machine ID' has very high importance, far above sensor readings like temperature and vibration. What should the team investigate first?
options: Whether machine ID is acting as a proxy for a specific faulty machine or batch, which may or may not generalize to future machines
Whether to immediately deploy the model into production without any further checks, since high importance implies high accuracy
Whether all of the sensor readings should simply be deleted from the dataset entirely
Whether every defective unit in the dataset should be re-labeled as non-defective
explanation: A categorical identifier like machine ID dominating importance could reflect a genuine effect (one bad machine) or an artifact that will not generalize once new machines are added, so it needs targeted investigation before trusting the model.

q: Which of the following is a known caveat when interpreting tree-based feature importance scores?
options: Highly correlated features can split importance between them, making each look individually less important than it really is
Feature importance is always identical to the correlation coefficient with the target
Feature importance scores are guaranteed to sum to exactly 1 only for regression tasks
Feature importance scores simply cannot ever be computed at all for categorical input features, in any implementation whatsoever
explanation: When two features carry similar information, trees may alternate between them across different splits and trees, diluting each one's individual importance score even though together they are highly predictive.

q: Refer to the feature-importance chart below for a credit card fraud model.
options: This indicates possible data leakage or an over-dominant feature, since one input drives the overwhelming majority of decisions
This indicates a perfectly balanced and fully trustworthy model with no concerns
This indicates that the model simply has far too few input features available to ever be useful for anything at all in practice
This indicates that the model is badly underfitting the available training data
explanation: A single feature with importance far above all others is a warning sign worth investigating for leakage (e.g., a feature that encodes the outcome indirectly) rather than evidence of a healthy, generalizable model.

q: Refer to the feature-importance chart below for a customer-churn model trained on behavioral and account data.
options: The importance is fairly balanced across several plausible churn drivers, suggesting a reasonably healthy model rather than one shortcut
The chart shows the model is relying entirely on just one single leaked input feature, ignoring all four of the other features entirely
The chart somehow proves the model will achieve 100% accuracy on brand-new data
The chart shows that none of the five features matter to the model at all
explanation: When importance is spread across multiple sensible features rather than concentrated in one, it is a healthier sign that the model is combining several real signals instead of exploiting a single artifact.
